change.describe: branch `pr-80329-flat` of grafana-80329-flat against a886bd3c79a417a70b51509384d1f1ec3e87e96b (merge-base a886bd3)
change.title: pr-80329-flat
change.author: Cristian Sotomayor

findings.title: Cleanup ticker cut from 10 minutes to 1 minute for every cleanup job
findings.body: This ticker drives every job in `clean` (lines 96-105): snapshots, dashboard versions, images, annotations, invites, short URLs and query history. Changing it from 10 minutes to 1 minute makes each Grafana instance run all of them ten times as often. `clean` takes no server lock, so in an HA setup every instance does this. The 9-minute timeout at line 89 was sized for the 10-minute interval. With a 1-minute tick, a slow run is followed by the next run right away, so cleanup can keep the database busy almost all the time. The PR body talks about annotation deadlocks and performance, not about how often cleanup runs, so this looks like a debugging change left in. Please revert it to `time.Minute * 10`.

findings.title: Debug logging at Error level dumps every ID list on each cleanup run
findings.body: Lines 534, 537, 554, 557, 576 and 579 call `r.log.Error` on every batch, including when nothing is deleted. Each line includes the full `ids` slice (up to `cleanupjob_batchsize`, 100 by default per setting.go:710, and up to 32767 in the new test) plus the raw SQL condition. `CleanOrphanedAnnotationTags` runs on every cleanup cycle, so at least two Error lines go out each run even when there is nothing to delete, and with the ticker change that is every minute. Error-level noise like this sets off log-based alerting and hides real errors. Also, the `err` logged at 534/554/576 is always nil because of the check just above. These lines should be removed or moved to Debug without the ID list.

findings.title: Building the inlined SQLite ID list is quadratic
findings.body: `values = fmt.Sprintf("%s, %d", values, v)` copies the whole string it has built so far on every ID. At the batch size this branch exists for (more than 999, and 32767 in the test), that is gigabytes of copying per batch. Use `strings.Builder` with `strconv.AppendInt`, or `strings.Join` over formatted IDs, so the cost stays linear.

findings.title: "running the max count delete again" no longer runs anything again
findings.body: Each subtest now creates its own data (line 116) and deletes all rows in `t.Cleanup` (lines 120-127). This case therefore starts from 9 new annotations (3 per type) and never repeats an earlier max-count run. It checks that a table already at MaxCount is left alone, not that a second run is a no-op. Rename it, or have it call `cleaner.Run` twice on the same data.

contracts.action: Time-based annotation cleanup now fetches IDs (SELECT ... created < cutoff ORDER BY id DESC LIMIT n) and then deletes by ID in a separate statement
contracts.equivalent_path: Previous single-statement DELETE ... WHERE id IN (SELECT id FROM (SELECT ... LIMIT n) a) run through executeUntilDoneOrCancelled
contracts.before_after: Both loop until a batch affects 0 rows, the context is cancelled or an error occurs. The new code does not re-check `created < cutoff` at delete time, but `created` is fixed for a given ID, so the IDs fetched still match the condition.
contracts.visible_effect: Old annotations disappear from dashboards. The count goes up the chain through Run to cleanUpOldAnnotations, which logs it at Debug.
contracts.failure_mode: A fetch or delete error returns the total so far plus the error. cleanUpOldAnnotations logs anything except DeadlineExceeded. Rows that are not deleted are picked up on the next cycle.

contracts.action: Count-based cleanup fetches the IDs past offset MaxCount, then deletes them by ID
contracts.equivalent_path: Previous single DELETE using LimitOffset inside the subquery
contracts.before_after: Nothing checks the fetched IDs again before the delete. A concurrent insert only pushes them further past the offset, so it is safe. If a user deletes newer annotations between the fetch and the delete, a fetched ID can fall back inside the top MaxCount and still get deleted. That leaves a few fewer than MaxCount, and only during that short window.
contracts.visible_effect: Excess annotations per type are removed.
contracts.failure_mode: Errors stop the loop and are returned. The previous code returned at this point anyway, so the change at 561-563 does not change behaviour.

contracts.action: Orphaned annotation_tag rows are fetched by NOT EXISTS and then deleted by ID
contracts.equivalent_path: Previous single DELETE with NOT EXISTS subquery
contracts.before_after: A tag fetched as orphaned stays orphaned. The parent annotation ID it points to has been deleted, and IDs are not handed out again for new rows inserted alongside it.
contracts.visible_effect: None to users. The tag count is returned to Run.
contracts.failure_mode: Errors are returned and the next cycle tries again.

contracts.action: Cleanup background loop ticks every minute instead of every 10 minutes
contracts.equivalent_path: Previous 10-minute ticker, with the 9-minute timeout in clean()
contracts.before_after: clean() runs every cleanup job one after another under a 9-minute timeout and takes no server lock, so a 1-minute tick makes all jobs run ten times as often on every instance.
contracts.visible_effect: More database load. The new Error logs show up in server logs every minute.
contracts.failure_mode: If a run takes more than a minute, the next tick fires right after it ends and runs start back to back.

summary: The fetch-then-delete-by-ID rewrite holds up. Each cleanup phase loops until a batch deletes nothing, and the delete targets stay valid: `created` is fixed for a given ID, and an orphaned tag stays orphaned. Two debugging leftovers should not ship. First, the cleanup ticker for all jobs drops from 10 minutes to 1 minute, which runs every cleanup job ten times as often on every instance. That is a blocker. Second, six `log.Error` calls dump full ID lists on every batch, even when nothing is deleted. Smaller points: the SQLite ID-inlining path builds its string in quadratic time, and one test name no longer describes what the test does.
